name: Cartalax

lead: Cartalax is a short synthetic peptide (alanine-glutamate-aspartate) developed in Russia by Vladimir Khavinson's group. People use it hoping to support cartilage and joints.
Lab studies have looked at its effect on kidney cells, skin fibroblasts and stem cells.

paras: In cultured cells, the peptide influenced proliferation and aging-related markers and gene expression. How this relates to joints in people has not been studied.
No human safety data are published. It is a research-grade peptide sold online, not an approved medicine.

news.title: Cartilage - Specific Signaling : Cartalax Peptide Across Connective Tissue Biology

chain: Short peptide studied for effects on cartilage and ageing cells
Aimed at joint and connective-tissue upkeep
More comfortable training and a longer-lasting physique
angle.text: Users take it hoping for healthier joints and connective tissue so they can keep lifting and stay youthful-looking. Lab studies on cartilage cells and skin fibroblasts are the basis for the joint and skin-ageing interest.

lead: Cartalax, also written AED or T-31, is a synthetic tripeptide made of alanine, glutamate and aspartate. It was developed in Russia, and most of the published work comes from the group of gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson, who studied short peptides as 'bioregulators'.[1][2] People interested in joint and connective-tissue upkeep use it in the hope of keeping cartilage comfortable, which in turn lets them keep training and maintain a muscular, youthful physique; its skin-fibroblast research also gives it a place in anti-ageing skin discussions.[1]

In the laboratory, AED has been tested on human mesenchymal stem cells and chondrocytes (cartilage cells) during replicative ageing, on human skin fibroblasts, and in rats with kidney injury. In stem cells, AED raised gene and protein markers of cartilage formation, including SOX9, aggrecan, type II collagen and COMP.[3] In aged chondrocytes it normalised markers of an inflammatory ageing phenotype.[4] In skin fibroblasts it increased sirtuin-1, sirtuin-6 and collagen I synthesis.[5]
Published work consists of cell-culture and animal studies. Wikipedia reports that limited human studies exist and describes ageing and arthritis claims as promotional.[1]
infobox: Sold as a supplement-type product in Russian-speaking countries and online[1]

paras: Cartalax is the three-amino-acid sequence alanine-glutamate-aspartate. Its molecular formula is C12H19N3O8, with a molar mass of about 333 g/mol.[1] It is sold in Russian-speaking countries and online as an anti-ageing and joint-support product.[1]

The St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, directed by Vladimir Khavinson (1946-2024), is associated with a family of short peptide bioregulators. Wikipedia credits him with developing peptide-based preparations aimed at slowing ageing and notes that several of its claims about safety rest on sources he authored.[2]

Cartilage: in human mesenchymal stem cells undergoing replicative ageing, AED at a test concentration of 200 ng/ml activated gene expression and protein synthesis of SOX9, aggrecan, type II collagen and COMP, markers of cartilage-type differentiation. The authors said this opens prospects for further work in osteoarthritis models.[3] A companion study found that AED and a cartilage polypeptide complex normalised markers in aged chondrocytes, including p16, p21, p53, TNF-alpha, IL-1 alpha and Sirt1.[4]

Skin: in human skin fibroblasts during replicative ageing, AED increased sirtuin-1, sirtuin-6 and collagen I synthesis, which the authors described as a geroprotective effect; a related peptide, KE, reduced inflammatory markers.[5]
Kidney: in rats with cisplatin-induced kidney failure, AED reduced protein and electrolyte excretion in urine, while other peptides had broader effects.[6]

sections.h: Use in recovery and anti-ageing circles
paras: Khavinson-style peptides are discussed in longevity and recovery communities as alternatives to larger peptide therapies. Marketing in some markets lists arthritis among its uses, which Wikipedia describes as supported by only limited human studies.[1] Forum discussion of peptides for recovery on sites such as T Nation focuses mainly on other compounds.
Wikipedia's article carries no adverse-effect information for Cartalax,[1] and no human safety trials were located.
No studies found in humans. The research described above is in cell cultures and animals, mostly from the originating Russian group.[3][4][5][6]

lore.intro: In recovery and anti-ageing circles Cartalax is described as a cartilage-targeted short peptide from the Russian bioregulator school.[1]

claims.claim: Cartalax supports cartilage and joint health

timeline.event: Rat study reports effects of AED among short peptides in cisplatin-induced kidney failure.[6]
Study of AED in aging human skin fibroblasts reports increased sirtuin and collagen I synthesis.[5]
Studies report AED effects on chondrogenic markers in aged stem cells and on chondrocyte ageing phenotype.[3][4]
